claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: TGF-β signaling is deregulated in diverse pathologies.
claims.source: In addition, their signaling is deregulated in diverse pathologies (Miller and Hill, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to review literature.

claims.claim: TGF-β ligands exert their action by binding to type I and type II serine/threonine kinase receptors at the cell surface.
claims.source: They exert their action by binding to type I and type II serine/threonine kinase receptors at the cell surface (TGFBR1 and TGFBR2, respectively, for the TGF-βs) (Massagué, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: In the ligand-bound heterotetrameric receptor complex, the type II receptor phosphorylates and activates the type I receptor.
claims.source: In the resulting ligand-bound heterotetrameric receptor complex, the type II receptor phosphorylates and activates the type I receptor, which in turn phosphorylates the intracellular mediators, the receptor-regulated SMADs (R-SMADs).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about TGF-β signaling mechanism.

claims.claim: The type I receptor phosphorylates the receptor-regulated SMADs (R-SMADs).
claims.source: In the resulting ligand-bound heterotetrameric receptor complex, the type II receptor phosphorylates and activates the type I receptor, which in turn phosphorylates the intracellular mediators, the receptor-regulated SMADs (R-SMADs).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about TGF-β signaling mechanism.

claims.claim: Once phosphorylated, R-SMADs (SMAD2 and SMAD3 in the case of TGF-β, Activin, and Nodal) associate with SMAD4.
claims.source: Once phosphorylated, the R-SMADs (SMAD2 and SMAD3 in the case of TGF-β, Activin, and Nodal) associate with the common mediator of the pathway, SMAD4.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about TGF-β signaling mechanism.

claims.claim: Heterotrimeric R-SMAD–SMAD4 complexes accumulate in the nucleus where they interact with other transcriptional regulators to activate or repress target gene expression.
claims.source: The resulting heterotrimeric complexes accumulate in the nucleus where they interact with other transcriptional regulators to activate or repress target gene expression (Massagué, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: SKI and SKIL act as negative regulators in the TGF-β pathway.
claims.source: Two highly related co-repressors, SKI and SKIL (formerly known as SnoN), act as negative regulators in the pathway (Deheuninck and Luo, 2009; see below).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation and demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: MFS is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the extracellular matrix protein, Fibrillin 1 (FBN1).
claims.source: MFS is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the extracellular matrix protein, Fibrillin 1 (FBN1) (Dietz et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: FBN1 mutations are thought to increase the bioavailability of TGF-β ligands, as FBN1 binds the latent form of the TGF-βs.
claims.source: These mutations are thought to increase the bioavailability of TGF-β ligands, as FBN1 binds the latent form of the TGF-βs (Neptune et al., 2003; Kaartinen and Warburton, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations.

claims.claim: A TGF-β neutralizing antibody significantly improved the lung phenotype in a mouse model of MFS (homozygous Fbn1mgΔ).
claims.source: Supporting the idea that excessive TGF-β signaling contributes to the manifestations of MFS, a TGF-β neutralizing antibody significantly improved the lung phenotype in a mouse model of MFS (homozygous Fbn1mgΔ) (Neptune et al., 2003; Cannaerts et al., 2015) and reduced the occurrence of aortic aneurysms in the Fbn1C1039G/+ mouse model of MFS (Habashi et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: A TGF-β neutralizing antibody reduced the occurrence of aortic aneurysms in the Fbn1C1039G/+ mouse model of MFS.
claims.source: Supporting the idea that excessive TGF-β signaling contributes to the manifestations of MFS, a TGF-β neutralizing antibody significantly improved the lung phenotype in a mouse model of MFS (homozygous Fbn1mgΔ) (Neptune et al., 2003; Cannaerts et al., 2015) and reduced the occurrence of aortic aneurysms in the Fbn1C1039G/+ mouse model of MFS (Habashi et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claims.claim: The aortopathy in the Fbn1C1039G/+ mouse model is not mediated by excessive TGF-β signaling and is exacerbated by loss of TGF-β signaling in smooth muscle cells.
claims.source: Contradicting these results, others have shown that the aortopathy in the Fbn1C1039G/+ mouse model is not mediated by excessive TGF-β signaling and in fact is exacerbated by loss of TGF-β signaling in smooth muscle cells (Wei et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claims.claim: TGF-β signaling protects against abdominal aortic aneurysms in angiotensin II-infused mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, TGF-β signaling protects against abdominal aortic aneurysms in angiotensin II-infused mice (Angelov et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claims.claim: LDS is caused by pathogenic mutations in TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD2, SMAD3, TGFB2, and TGFB3.
claims.source: Furthermore, the related syndrome LDS is caused by pathogenic mutations in several different components of the TGF-β pathway, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD2, SMAD3, and the ligands, TGFB2 and TGFB3.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: LDS mutations all cause missense amino acid substitutions that have been either verified in vitro, or are predicted to be loss of function.
claims.source: These mutations all cause missense amino acid substitutions that have been either verified in vitro, or are predicted to be loss of function, implying that LDS is caused by attenuated TGF-β signaling (Horbelt et al., 2010; Cardoso et al., 2012; Schepers et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Histological and biochemical studies of aortic tissue derived from LDS patients reveal an apparent high TGF-β signaling signature.
claims.source: However, paradoxically, histological and biochemical studies of aortic tissue derived from LDS patients reveal an apparent high TGF-β signaling signature (van de Laar et al., 2012; Gallo et al., 2014; Lindsay et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Both SMAD-mediated and non-SMAD-mediated TGF-β signaling has been reported to be increased in primary dermal fibroblasts from SGS patients.
claims.source: SGS is caused by mutations in SKI, and both SMAD-mediated and non-SMAD-mediated TGF-β signaling has been reported to be increased in primary dermal fibroblasts from SGS patients (Doyle et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: SKI and SKIL play important roles in proliferation, differentiation, transformation, and tumor progression.
claims.source: The co-repressors SKI and SKIL play important roles in a number of different cellular processes including proliferation, differentiation, transformation, and tumor progression (Bonnon and Atanasoski, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to review literature.

claims.claim: SKI and SKIL are dimeric proteins that interact with both phosphorylated SMAD2 and SMAD3 via short motifs at their N-termini.
claims.source: They are dimeric proteins that interact with both phosphorylated SMAD2 and SMAD3 (PSMAD2 or PSMAD3) via short motifs at their N-termini, and with SMAD4 via a SAND domain (named after Sp100, AIRE-1, NucP41/75, DEAF-1) in the middle of both proteins (Deheuninck and Luo, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: SKI and SKIL interact with SMAD4 via a SAND domain in the middle of both proteins.
claims.source: They are dimeric proteins that interact with both phosphorylated SMAD2 and SMAD3 (PSMAD2 or PSMAD3) via short motifs at their N-termini, and with SMAD4 via a SAND domain (named after Sp100, AIRE-1, NucP41/75, DEAF-1) in the middle of both proteins (Deheuninck and Luo, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: The Dachshund homology domain (DHD) in SKI and SKIL is thought to be important for R-SMAD binding.
claims.source: Between these two domains lies a Dachshund homology domain (DHD), which is thought to also be important for R-SMAD binding (Wilson et al., 2004; Ueki and Hayman, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: SKI and SKIL contain a leucine zipper domain in their C-termini, through which they dimerize.
claims.source: SKI and SKIL both contain a leucine zipper domain in their C-termini, through which they dimerize (Deheuninck and Luo, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: SKI and SKIL bind with SMAD4 to SMAD binding elements (SBEs) of TGF-β/Activin target genes, and recruit co-repressors such as NCOR1 or SIN3A.
claims.source: In one model, SKI and SKIL bind with SMAD4 to SMAD binding elements (SBEs) of TGF-β/Activin target genes, and recruit co-repressors such as NCOR1 or SIN3A (Tokitou et al., 1999; Nomura et al., 1999; Stroschein et al., 1999; Deheuninck and Luo, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is one proposed mechanism supported by citations.

claims.claim: Upon TGF-β/Activin signaling, SKI and SKIL are rapidly degraded by the E3 ubiquitin ligase, RNF111, a process that requires SKI/SKIL binding to PSMAD2 or PSMAD3.
claims.source: Upon TGF-β/Activin signaling, SKI and SKIL are rapidly degraded by the E3 ubiquitin ligase, RNF111 (formerly known as Arkadia), a process that requires SKI/SKIL binding to PSMAD2 or PSMAD3 (Le Scolan et al., 2008; Levy et al., 2007; Nagano et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Degradation of SKI and SKIL allows activated SMAD3–SMAD4 complexes to bind the exposed SBEs and activate target gene transcription.
claims.source: This then allows the activated SMAD3–SMAD4 complexes to bind the exposed SBEs and activate target gene transcription (Levy et al., 2007; Stroschein et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The heterozygous missense mutations that cause SGS have been mapped in SKI to the N-terminal R-SMAD-binding domain, with some small deletions and point mutations also found in the DHD.
claims.source: The heterozygous missense mutations that cause SGS have been mapped in SKI to the N-terminal R-SMAD-binding domain, with some small deletions and point mutations also found in the DHD, which is also necessary for R-SMAD binding (Carmignac et al., 2012; Doyle et al., 2012; Schepers et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Deletion of SMAD4 in HEK293T and HaCaT cells abolished ligand-induced SKI/SKIL degradation.
claims.source: Deletion of SMAD4 in multiple clones of both cell types abolished ligand-induced SKI/SKIL degradation (Figure 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 1A and 1B showing SKI/SKIL levels remain unchanged after TGF-β/Activin treatment in SMAD4 knockout cells.

claims.claim: Knockout of SMAD2 or SMAD3 individually or together abolished TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI and SKIL.
claims.source: By knocking out SMAD2 or SMAD3 individually or together, we also confirmed that these R-SMADs are absolutely required for TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI and SKIL and act redundantly (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 1C showing SKI/SKIL levels remain unchanged after Activin treatment in SMAD2/SMAD3 knockout cells.

claims.claim: SMAD2 and SMAD3 act redundantly in TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI and SKIL.
claims.source: By knocking out SMAD2 or SMAD3 individually or together, we also confirmed that these R-SMADs are absolutely required for TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI and SKIL and act redundantly (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that knockout of either SMAD2 or SMAD3 alone is sufficient to block SKI/SKIL degradation.

claims.claim: R-SMADs and SMAD4 are all essential for TGF-β/Activin-dependent SKI/SKIL degradation.
claims.source: Thus, R-SMADs and SMAD4 are all essential for TGF-β/Activin-dependent SKI/SKIL degradation.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the knockout experiments shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Amino acids 11–45 of SKI are sufficient for binding to PSMAD2 and PSMAD3 upon TGF-β stimulation.
claims.source: This revealed that amino acids 11–45 of SKI are sufficient for binding to PSMAD2 and PSMAD3 upon TGF-β stimulation, whilst the unphosphorylated SMADs did not bind to any of the SKI peptides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide pulldown assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Unphosphorylated SMADs do not bind to SKI peptides.
claims.source: This revealed that amino acids 11–45 of SKI are sufficient for binding to PSMAD2 and PSMAD3 upon TGF-β stimulation, whilst the unphosphorylated SMADs did not bind to any of the SKI peptides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide pulldown assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Six different SGS mutations in the SKI peptide 11–45 prevented binding of PSMAD2 and PSMAD3.
claims.source: To determine the effect of these mutations on R-SMAD interaction, we introduced six different SGS mutations into the SKI peptide 11–45 and showed that they all prevented binding of PSMAD2 and PSMAD3, and as a result, also SMAD4 (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide pulldown assays shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: SGS mutations in SKIL (equivalent to those in SKI) prevented binding of PSMAD2 and PSMAD3.
claims.source: These results were also confirmed with the equivalent mutations in SKIL (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide pulldown assays shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The interaction of SKI with SMAD2 is mediated via the SMAD2 MH2 domain.
claims.source: We proved that the interaction with SMAD2 was mediated via its MH2 domain using a mouse embryonic fibroblast cell line that expresses a truncated SMAD2 protein comprising just the MH2 domain (Piek et al., 2001; Das et al., 2009; Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide pulldown assays shown in Figure 4C and 4D using SMAD2 MH2 domain.

claims.claim: Eight residues in SKI (Thr20, Leu21, Phe24, Ser28, Ser31, Leu32, Gly34, and Pro35) are intolerant to almost any amino acid substitution for PSMAD3–SMAD4 binding.
claims.source: Eight residues are intolerant to almost any amino acid substitution (Thr20, Leu21, Phe24, Ser28, Ser31, Leu32, Gly34, and Pro35).
claims.evidence: This is determined from the peptide array shown in Figure 4E and quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Six of the eight crucial residues for R-SMAD binding (Leu21, Ser28, Ser31, Leu32, Gly34, and Pro35) are amino acids known to be mutated in SGS patients.
claims.source: Strikingly, six of these residues are the amino acids known to be mutated in SGS patients, and the array results readily explain why these residues are mutated to a number of different amino acids in SGS (Figure 4E; for quantification, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the peptide array data in Figure 4E showing these residues are critical for binding.

claims.claim: The crystal structure of the SKI peptide with the phosphorylated SMAD2 MH2 domain was determined at 2 Å resolution.
claims.source: The structure was determined by molecular replacement and refined at 2 Å resolution and readily explained why the crucial amino acids identified in the peptide were required for SMAD2 binding (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The dissociation constant (Kd) of the SKI peptide to the SMAD2 MH2 domain trimer is in the low nanomolar range.
claims.source: Analysis of the binding affinity of the SKI peptide to the SMAD2 MH2 domain trimer indicated that the dissociation constant (Kd) was in the low nanomolar range (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by biolayer interferometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The SKI peptide binds on the outside face of the SMAD2 MH2 domain at the three helix bundle, comprising helices 3, 4, and 5.
claims.source: The SKI peptide binds on the outside face of the MH2 domain at the so-called three helix bundle, comprising helices 3, 4, and 5 (Wu et al., 2001; Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: SKI can only bind SMAD2 in its phosphorylated trimeric state.
claims.source: Thus, SKI can only bind SMAD2 in its phosphorylated trimeric state.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from structural comparison shown in Figure 5G and 5H, demonstrating that Trp448 is in the correct orientation for SKI binding only in the trimeric state.

claims.claim: In three independent clonal cell lines carrying the P35S SKI mutation, the binding to endogenous phosphorylated SMAD2 was severely compromised, compared with WT SKI.
claims.source: In three independent clonal cell lines carrying the P35S SKI mutation, the binding to endogenous phosphorylated SMAD2 was severely compromised, compared with WT SKI (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The binding of P35S SKI to SMAD4 was unchanged compared to WT SKI.
claims.source: The binding to SMAD4, however, was unchanged in the mutant cell lines, as the SGS mutations do not affect the SKI SAND domain, which is responsible for SMAD4 binding (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: P35S SKI levels remained stable after Activin treatment, whilst WT SKI protein is almost entirely degraded after 1 hr of Activin treatment.
claims.source: At both time points, we clearly demonstrated that P35S SKI levels remained stable, whilst in the parental cell lines, SKI protein is almost entirely degraded after 1 hr of Activin treatment (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The presence of mutated SKI had no effect on the Activin-induced degradation of SKIL.
claims.source: The presence of mutated SKI had no effect on the Activin-induced degradation of SKIL in these lines (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The P35S mutation renders SKI completely resistant to ligand-induced degradation.
claims.source: Thus, the P35S mutation renders SKI completely resistant to ligand-induced degradation.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the Western blot data in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: After Activin stimulation, the binding of WT SKI to SBEs is lost, whilst the binding of P35S SKI is retained.
claims.source: Consistent with our prediction, both WT and P35S SKI bound the SBEs with SMAD4 in the absence of signal, but after Activin stimulation, the binding of WT SKI is lost, whilst the binding of P35S SKI is retained (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA pulldown assay shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: There was a significant reduction in Activin-induced CAGA12-Luciferase activity in the P35S SKI cells compared to the parental cell line.
claims.source: Strikingly, we found a significant reduction in Activin-induced CAGA12-Luciferase activity in the P35S SKI cells compared to the parental cell line (Figure 6D), while BMP4-induced BRE-Luciferase activity was similar in all cell lines (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: BMP4-induced BRE-Luciferase activity was similar in P35S SKI cells and parental cells.
claims.source: Strikingly, we found a significant reduction in Activin-induced CAGA12-Luciferase activity in the P35S SKI cells compared to the parental cell line (Figure 6D), while BMP4-induced BRE-Luciferase activity was similar in all cell lines (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: SGS mutations in SKI lead to inhibition of TGF-β/Activin-induced transcription mediated by PSMAD3–SMAD4 complexes.
claims.source: The results indicate that SGS mutations in SKI lead to inhibition of TGF-β/Activin-induced transcription mediated by PSMAD3–SMAD4 complexes.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: In control fibroblasts, SKI expression is abrogated upon TGF-β stimulation after 1 hr, while in the SGS-derived fibroblasts, SKI protein remains relatively stable.
claims.source: Indeed, in control fibroblasts, SKI expression is abrogated upon TGF-β stimulation after 1 hr, while in the SGS-derived fibroblasts, SKI protein remains relatively stable (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Of the 339 genes that were differentially expressed in normal fibroblasts after 1 hr of TGF-β treatment, 60% (202 genes) were induced or repressed less efficiently in the L32V mutant fibroblasts.
claims.source: We found that of the 339 genes that were differentially expressed in normal fibroblasts after 1 hr of TGF-β treatment, 60% (202 genes) were induced or repressed less efficiently in the L32V mutant fibroblasts, and of these, 97 genes were not significantly differentially expressed in the mutant cells at all (Figure 7—source data 1, Figure 7B,C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claims.claim: Of the 339 genes differentially expressed in normal fibroblasts after 1 hr of TGF-β treatment, 97 genes were not significantly differentially expressed in the L32V mutant cells.
claims.source: We found that of the 339 genes that were differentially expressed in normal fibroblasts after 1 hr of TGF-β treatment, 60% (202 genes) were induced or repressed less efficiently in the L32V mutant fibroblasts, and of these, 97 genes were not significantly differentially expressed in the mutant cells at all (Figure 7—source data 1, Figure 7B,C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claims.claim: After an 8 hr TGF-β induction, 4769 genes were differentially expressed in the normal fibroblasts, and of these 75% (3556 genes) were induced or repressed less efficiently in the L32V mutant cells.
claims.source: After an 8 hr TGF-β induction, we found that 4769 genes were differentially expressed in the normal fibroblasts, and of these 75% (3556 genes) were induced or repressed less efficiently in the L32V mutant cells, and 880 genes were not significantly differentially expressed in the mutant cells at all (Figure 7—source data 1, Figure 7B,C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claims.claim: After an 8 hr TGF-β induction, 880 genes were not significantly differentially expressed in the L32V mutant cells.
claims.source: After an 8 hr TGF-β induction, we found that 4769 genes were differentially expressed in the normal fibroblasts, and of these 75% (3556 genes) were induced or repressed less efficiently in the L32V mutant cells, and 880 genes were not significantly differentially expressed in the mutant cells at all (Figure 7—source data 1, Figure 7B,C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claims.claim: The presence of SGS point mutations in SKI that render it resistant to ligand-induced degradation result in attenuated TGF-β responses for a substantial subset of target genes.
claims.source: Thus, we conclude that the presence of SGS point mutations in SKI that render it resistant to ligand-induced degradation, result in attenuated TGF-β responses for a substantial subset of target genes.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B, C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D.

claims.claim: In unstimulated cells, SKI and SKIL interact with the E3 ubiquitin ligase, RNF111, although this binding per se does not lead to SKI/SKIL degradation.
claims.source: We and others have also shown that in unstimulated cells, SKI and SKIL interact with the E3 ubiquitin ligase, RNF111, although this binding per se does not lead to SKI/SKIL degradation (Le Scolan et al., 2008; Levy et al., 2007; Nagano et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: An intact functional phosphorylated R-SMAD–SMAD4 trimer is required to bind to SKIL to induce its ligand-dependent degradation.
claims.source: Second, we clearly demonstrate for the first time that an intact functional phosphorylated R-SMAD–SMAD4 trimer is required to bind to SKIL to induce its ligand-dependent degradation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the SMAD4 mutant rescue experiments shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: SMAD4 mutants that cannot form a canonical activated R-SMAD–SMAD4 trimer cannot rescue ligand-induced SKIL degradation.
claims.source: Critically, we show that SMAD4 mutants that cannot form a canonical activated R-SMAD–SMAD4 trimer cannot rescue ligand-induced SKIL degradation, neither can SMAD4 mutants that do not interact with the SAND domain of SKIL.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claims.claim: SMAD4 mutants that do not interact with the SAND domain of SKIL cannot rescue ligand-induced SKIL degradation.
claims.source: Critically, we show that SMAD4 mutants that cannot form a canonical activated R-SMAD–SMAD4 trimer cannot rescue ligand-induced SKIL degradation, neither can SMAD4 mutants that do not interact with the SAND domain of SKIL.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claims.claim: TGF-β/Activin-induced SKIL degradation occurs only when SKIL interacts simultaneously with phosphorylated R-SMADs and with SMAD4, which in turn must interact with each other in a transcriptionally active trimer.
claims.source: Thus, we conclude that TGF-β/Activin-induced SKIL degradation occurs only when SKIL interacts simultaneously with phosphorylated R-SMADs and with SMAD4, which in turn must interact with each other in a transcriptionally active trimer.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the SMAD4 mutant rescue experiments shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: SKIL binding to the R-SMAD–SMAD4 complex does not disrupt it.
claims.source: This strongly indicates that SKIL binding to the R-SMAD–SMAD4 complex does not disrupt it.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for an intact R-SMAD–SMAD4 complex for SKIL degradation.

claims.claim: The crystal structure of the SAND domain of SKIL with the SMAD4 MH2 domain revealed that SKIL interacts with SMAD4 in two states: an 'open' and a 'closed' conformation.
claims.source: This structure revealed that SKIL interacts with SMAD4 in two states: an 'open' and a 'closed' conformation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Walldén et al., 2017.

claims.claim: In the open conformation, SKIL can bind the R-SMAD–SMAD4 complex without intermolecular clashes or further structural readjustment.
claims.source: In the open conformation, the authors showed that SKIL can bind the R-SMAD–SMAD4 complex without intermolecular clashes or further structural readjustment, whereas in the closed state, structural reorganization within the SMAD heterotrimer is required to allow binding of SKIL, as has been observed in the previous structure of SKI with SMAD4 (Wu et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Walldén et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The open conformation is the biologically and functionally relevant mode of SKIL-SMAD4 binding.
claims.source: Furthermore, surface plasmon resonance indicated only one dominant binding mode for SKIL and SMAD4, leading to the conclusion that the open conformation is the biologically and functionally relevant mode and that the closed conformation may be the result of crystal packing forces (Walldén et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Walldén et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The residues that allow the binding in the open conformation are highly conserved between SKI and SKIL.
claims.source: Note that the residues that allow the binding in the open conformation are highly conserved between SKI and SKIL, suggesting that both repressors bind to an intact activated R-SMAD–SMAD4 complex, which is required for their degradation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from sequence conservation and structural data.

claims.claim: Patients with 1p36 deletion syndrome, who are haploinsufficient for SKI, do not have SGS.
claims.source: Finally, our finding that SGS mutations in SKI lead to its stabilization and are not equivalent to loss of SKI function also explains why patients with 1p36 deletion syndrome, who are haploinsufficient for SKI, do not have SGS.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Colmenares et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Many of the same organs are affected in both 1p36 deletion syndrome and SGS.
claims.source: However, unsurprisingly, many of the same organs are affected in both syndromes (Colmenares et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claims.claim: A PSMAD2/3–SMAD4 ternary complex is essential for TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI/SKIL.
claims.source: A PSMAD2/3–SMAD4 ternary complex is essential for TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI/SKIL
claims.evidence: This is the title of a results section and is demonstrated by the experiments in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claims.claim: The D351H and D537Y SMAD4 mutants lost their ability to bind SMAD2 upon TGF-β induction, but retained the interaction with SKIL.
claims.source: As predicted, the D351H and D537Y SMAD4 mutants had lost their ability to bind SMAD2 upon TGF-β induction, but retained the interaction with SKIL.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The A433E and I435Y SMAD4 mutants were unable to bind SKIL, but could interact with SMAD2 upon TGF-β stimulation.
claims.source: By contrast, A433E and I435Y SMAD4 mutants were unable to bind SKIL, but could interact with SMAD2 upon TGF-β stimulation (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The D351H and D537Y SMAD4 mutants failed to rescue the ability of TGF-β to induce expression of CAGA12-Luciferase in HaCaT SMAD4-null cells.

results.result: SGS is a multisystemic connective tissue disorder with clinical overlap with Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, caused by heterozygous mutations in SKI, a negative regulator of TGF-β signaling. All three syndromes have been linked to deregulation of TGF-β signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C8-C10 establish the clinical and molecular background of SGS based on established knowledge and prior literature. These claims are well-supported by citations to clinical and molecular studies and represent accepted knowledge in the field.

results.result: TGF-β family ligands play pleiotropic roles in development and homeostasis, and signal through type I and type II serine/threonine kinase receptors that phosphorylate R-SMADs, which then associate with SMAD4 to form heterotrimeric complexes that regulate gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C17 describe the canonical TGF-β signaling pathway, which is well-established knowledge supported by citations. These claims provide necessary background for understanding the experimental work.

results.result: SKI and SKIL are dimeric co-repressors that interact with phosphorylated SMAD2/3 via N-terminal motifs and with SMAD4 via a SAND domain, and act as negative regulators of TGF-β signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C29-C33 describe the structure and function of SKI/SKIL based on established knowledge and citations. These claims provide essential background for understanding the experimental findings.

results.result: MFS is caused by FBN1 mutations, with conflicting evidence regarding whether the syndrome results from excessive or attenuated TGF-β signaling, as different mouse models and interventions have produced contradictory results.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 accurately describe the controversy in the field regarding TGF-β signaling in MFS, supported by citations to both supporting and contradicting studies. This establishes the rationale for the current work.

results.result: LDS is caused by loss-of-function mutations in TGF-β pathway components, yet paradoxically, aortic tissue from LDS patients shows an apparent high TGF-β signaling signature.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 describe the paradox in LDS where genetic evidence suggests attenuated signaling but tissue analysis suggests enhanced signaling. This is well-supported by citations and establishes key context for the study.

results.result: Both SMAD-mediated and non-SMAD-mediated TGF-β signaling has been reported to be increased in primary dermal fibroblasts from SGS patients.
results.evaluation: Claim C28 cites prior work (Doyle et al., 2012) reporting increased TGF-β signaling in SGS patient fibroblasts, which the current study contradicts. This establishes the controversy the authors aim to resolve.

results.result: In one model of SKI/SKIL function, they bind with SMAD4 to SBEs and recruit co-repressors in the absence of signal, but are rapidly degraded by RNF111 upon TGF-β/Activin stimulation, allowing activated SMAD complexes to bind SBEs and activate transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 describe one proposed mechanism of SKI/SKIL action supported by citations. This model is subsequently validated by the authors' experimental work.

results.result: SGS mutations in SKI map to the N-terminal R-SMAD-binding domain and the DHD domain.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by citations to previous genetic studies identifying SGS mutations. This provides the foundation for the authors' structural and functional analysis.

results.result: SMAD4, SMAD2, and SMAD3 are all essential for TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI/SKIL, with SMAD2 and SMAD3 acting redundantly.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41, C80 are supported by Western blot data in Figure 1 showing that knockout of SMAD4, SMAD2, or SMAD3 abolishes ligand-induced SKI/SKIL degradation. The experiments include appropriate controls and multiple clones.

results.result: An intact functional phosphorylated R-SMAD-SMAD4 trimer is required for ligand-induced SKIL degradation. SMAD4 mutants that cannot bind R-SMADs or that cannot bind SKIL fail to rescue SKIL degradation, demonstrating that both interactions are essential and that SKIL binding does not disrupt the R-SMAD-SMAD4 complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73, C81-C89 are supported by comprehensive data in Figures 2 and 3 using SMAD4 mutants with defined binding defects. The experiments include immunoprecipitation, Western blot, flow cytometry, and immunofluorescence data, all showing consistent results across multiple assays.

results.result: Amino acids 11-45 of SKI are sufficient for binding to phosphorylated SMAD2/3 but not unphosphorylated SMADs. SGS mutations in this region prevent binding to phosphorylated R-SMADs, and these residues are completely conserved between species and in SKIL.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46, C90-C91 are supported by peptide pulldown assays in Figure 4 and sequence alignments in Figure 4-supplement 1A. The data clearly show that SGS mutations abolish R-SMAD binding while the interaction is mediated via the SMAD2 MH2 domain.

results.result: Eight residues in SKI (Thr20, Leu21, Phe24, Ser28, Ser31, Leu32, Gly34, Pro35) are intolerant to amino acid substitution for PSMAD3-SMAD4 binding, and six of these are mutated in SGS patients. The peptide array explains why these specific residues are mutated to various amino acids in SGS.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48, C92-C93 are supported by the comprehensive peptide array data in Figure 4E and quantification in Figure 4-supplement 1C. The array systematically tests all amino acid substitutions at each position, providing strong evidence for which residues are critical.

results.result: The crystal structure of the SKI peptide with phosphorylated SMAD2 MH2 domain trimer was determined at 2 Å resolution, revealing that SKI binds with low nanomolar affinity to the three helix bundle of SMAD2 through specific interactions involving the critical residues identified in the peptide array.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51, C94-C99 are supported by the crystal structure in Figure 5, SEC-MALLS data in Figure 5-supplement 1A, biolayer interferometry in Figure 5-supplement 1B, and crystallographic statistics in Figure 5-supplement 1C. The structure provides atomic-level detail explaining the binding interactions.

results.result: SKI can only bind SMAD2 in its phosphorylated trimeric state because trimerization causes Trp448 to move into an upright position compatible with SKI binding, whereas in the monomeric state Trp448 is in a flattened orientation incompatible with the required pi-stacking interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C100-C104 are supported by structural comparisons in Figure 5G-H and Video 1, showing the conformational changes in Trp448 and Tyr268 upon trimerization. This elegantly explains the specificity for phosphorylated trimeric R-SMADs.

results.result: In P35S SKI knockin cells, the mutation severely compromises binding to phosphorylated SMAD2 but not SMAD4, and renders SKI completely resistant to ligand-induced degradation while not affecting SKIL degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6A and Western blot data in Figure 6B showing that P35S SKI is stabilized after Activin treatment in multiple independent clones. The experiments include appropriate controls and time courses.

results.result: P35S SKI remains bound to SBEs with SMAD4 after Activin stimulation, leading to significant reduction in Activin-induced CAGA12-Luciferase activity but not BMP4-induced BRE-Luciferase activity, indicating that SGS mutations inhibit TGF-β/Activin-induced transcription mediated by PSMAD3-SMAD4 complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 are supported by DNA pulldown assays in Figure 6C and luciferase reporter assays in Figure 6D-E. The data show specific effects on TGF-β/Activin signaling but not BMP signaling, with statistical significance demonstrated across multiple experiments.

results.result: SGS mutations in SKIL (G103V) and SAND domain mutations that prevent SMAD4 binding both lead to resistance to Activin-induced degradation, demonstrating that both R-SMAD and SMAD4 interactions are essential for SKIL degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C108 are supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot data in Figure 6-supplement 1B-C. The experiments with SKIL mutants parallel the SKI results and confirm the generality of the mechanism.

results.result: In fibroblasts from SGS patients carrying L32V or ΔS94-97 mutations, SKI protein remains relatively stable after TGF-β stimulation. RNA-seq analysis shows that 60% of genes differentially expressed at 1 hr and 75% at 8 hr in normal fibroblasts are induced or repressed less efficiently in L32V mutant fibroblasts, demonstrating attenuated TGF-β responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C67 are supported by Western blot data in Figure 7A and comprehensive RNA-seq analysis in Figure 7B-C with four biological replicates. The data show consistent attenuation of TGF-β responses in patient fibroblasts, validating the findings from knockin cells in a clinically relevant context.

results.result: SGS mutations in SKI abolish binding to phosphorylated SMAD2/3, resulting in SKI stabilization and attenuation of TGF-β responses in both knockin cells and patient fibroblasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 represent the main conclusions of the study, which are supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence including peptide pulldowns (Figure 4), structural analysis (Figure 5), knockin cell studies (Figure 6), and patient fibroblast analysis (Figure 7). The conclusion that SGS leads to attenuated rather than enhanced TGF-β signaling is well-supported.

results.result: In unstimulated cells, SKI and SKIL interact with RNF111, but this binding alone does not lead to degradation.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors and others. This establishes that RNF111 binding is necessary but not sufficient for degradation.

results.result: The crystal structure of SKIL SAND domain with SMAD4 revealed open and closed conformations, with the open conformation being the biologically relevant mode that allows SKIL to bind an intact R-SMAD-SMAD4 complex without disruption.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by citation to Walldén et al., 2017 and are used to support the authors' model. The authors appropriately cite this prior structural work to explain how SKIL can bind without disrupting the SMAD complex.

results.result: Patients with 1p36 deletion syndrome who are haploinsufficient for SKI do not have SGS, though many of the same organs are affected, which is explained by the finding that SGS mutations lead to SKI stabilization rather than loss of function.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are supported by citations to clinical literature and represent a logical inference from the authors' findings. The distinction between haploinsufficiency and dominant-negative/gain-of-function effects is well-established.
